title: Attention kernel optimization profiling: FlashAttention, paged attention, fused ops - experiment log
content:
Summary:

This doc records profiling experiments comparing FlashAttention, paged attention, and fused attention operator implementations in our serving runtime. Goals: identify bottlenecks across sequence lengths and batch sizes, measure kernel-level speedups, verify memory/KV-cache interactions, and recommend a rollout plan for the runtime optimizer to pick kernels by workload profile.

High-level conclusions (TL;DR):
- FlashAttention provides 1.4-2.3x end-to-end token throughput improvement vs naive matmul-based attention on H100/A100 for medium-long sequences (512-2048), with the largest wins at seq len 1024.
- Paged attention reduces peak memory and improves tail latency in workloads with long context and sparsed KV cache reuse; throughput benefits are modest (1.05-1.2x) but enable stable latency SLOs for sequence >2048.
- Fused ops (fused qkv + attention + out projection kernels) yield significant CPU-GPU kernel fusion wins for small-batch, short-seq inference (batch 1-4, seq <= 128) — up to 1.6x token latency improvement by removing dispatch overheads and kernel launch latency.
- Primary bottlenecks observed: (1) memory-bound softmax reduction and attention score compute for very long sequences; (2) kernel launch overhead and small kernels dominating when batch size is small; (3) KV cache scatter/gather memory copy hotspots for paged designs.

Experimental setup:
- Hardware: NVidia H100 (PCIe 4.0) and A100 (80GB, PCIe) nodes in prod-like config; experiments repeated on both for cross-checking.
- Software: serving-runtime branch: attention-profiling-2026-03, CUDA 12.2 (H100), 11.8 (A100), cuBLAS/cuDNN matching vendor recommended, FlashAttention v2 (custom build), our paged attention prototype (in-runtime), fused-op kernels implemented in Triton/CUDA.
- Models: LLaMA-2-13B decoder-only model (fp16) converted to our runtime format; smaller 7B run for quick iteration.
- Workloads: synthetic single-request microbenchmarks and mixed workload trace replay from canary customers (anonymized). Key dimensions: batch size in {1,2,4,8,16}, seq len in {64,128,256,512,1024,2048,4096}, kv cache reuse ratio in {0.0,0.5,0.9} to simulate chat-style prefix reuse.
- Metrics captured: tokens/sec, p50/p95/p99 latency per token, GPU utilization, SM efficiency, achieved TFLOPs, peak device memory, kernel-level timeline (Nsight Systems), per-kernel GPU time (Nsight Compute), CPU-side scheduling overhead, PCIe memcpy time.

Key experiments & results:
1) FlashAttention vs baseline (matmul + softmax)
- Setup: batch=4, seq={256,512,1024}, model=13B, H100.
- Results: seq=256: +1.4x tokens/sec; seq=512: +1.9x; seq=1024: +2.3x.
- Observations: FlashAttention shifts compute from memory-bound softmax to more compute-bound fused kernels; SM utilization improves from ~42% to ~78% at seq=1024. Kernel timeline shows fewer large global memory reads.
- Notes: FlashAttention requires contiguous attention state which conflicts with some paged cache layouts - see integration caveats.

2) Paged attention memory & tail latency test
- Setup: batch=1, seq=4096, kv reuse=0.9, 13B, A100.
- Results: paged attention reduced peak device memory by ~28% and improved p99 latency by ~18% vs baseline (because paging reduced large memcpy spikes). End-to-end throughput change was small (~1.05x).
- Observations: paging reduces worst-case memory footprint enabling larger effective context; main overhead is scatter/gather CPU->GPU and additional small kernel invocations. Optimizing the scatter path (use pinned buffers + asynchronous memcpy streams) recovers much of the overhead.

3) Fused ops impact on small-batch latency-sensitive workloads
- Setup: batch=1, seq=64/128, 7B and 13B models, H100.
- Results: fused qkv + attention + out projection fused kernel reduced per-token p50 latency by 20-60% depending on sequence and model size; tokens/sec improved up to 1.6x for short-seq low-batch workloads.
- Observations: kernel launch overhead dominates when per-kernel workload is small. Fusion reduces host->device synchronization points. Triton implementation had better maintainability; custom CUDA kernel slightly faster (~5-10%) but at cost of complexity.

Bottleneck analysis (detailed):
- Long sequences (>=1024): memory bandwidth and softmax reduction dominate - FlashAttention's tiled approach and reduced global memory traffic are key. However, sustained TFLOPs still below theoretical peak when sequence length creates irregular memory accesses (sliced KV cache).
- Short sequences / small batches: kernel launch latency & CPU scheduling (driver) are the dominant factor. Fused kernels and persistent kernels (where applicable) help.
- KV cache management: paged KV layout reduces memory pressure but introduces scatter/gather hotspots and more frequent small memcpy operations. Using pinned memory + overlapped async copies reduced CPU-side stalls in our runs.
- Mixed workloads: smart routing (route short-batch requests to fused-op instances; long-context to FlashAttention/paged nodes) gives the best global throughput and latency balance.

Integration caveats & compatibility notes:
- FlashAttention v2 requires contiguous Q/K/V buffers and specific padding alignment; need a compatibility shim in the runtime for models with per-layer packing variations.
- Paged attention affects how we persist KV cache across requests; must ensure correctness for batched requests with heterogeneous context lengths - this increases shuffle complexity.
- Fused kernels complicate our observability (per-op token attribution) because multiple logical ops are collapsed into a single kernel; add tracing markers in the runtime to preserve high-level metrics.

Recommended rollout plan for optimizer (proposal):
- Phase 1 (canary): Enable FlashAttention on dedicated H100 pool for seq len >= 256 and batch >= 2. Monitor correctness and latency regressions for first 2 weeks.
- Phase 2: Enable fused kernels for latency-sensitive routes (batch <= 4, seq <= 128) on a short-seq node pool. Keep fallback to baseline kernels if p99 latency or correctness fails.
- Phase 3: Introduce paged attention as an opt-in feature for customers requiring >2048 context; default disabled for hosted API until we have robust scatter/gather async memcpy improvements and end-to-end tests.
- Routing policy: implement kernel selection policy that selects kernel based on (seq_len, batch_size, kv_reuse_hint, customer_tier). Keep A/B testing to measure production effect.

Open action items / TODOs:
- [ ] Add pinned buffer + async memcpy optimization for paged attention scatter/gather (owner: Aisha) - PR: #487
- [ ] Build compatibility shim for FlashAttention contiguous buffer requirement (owner: Daniel)
- [ ] Add tracing markers for fused kernels to preserve per-op metrics (owner: Miguel)
- [ ] Run 7-day canary of FlashAttention on H100 dedicated pool with real traffic replay (owner: eng-serving-runtime ops)
- [ ] Prepare customer-facing notes for enterprise customers about paged attention opt-in and memory/perf tradeoffs (owner: product-hosted-api)

Appendix: useful commands and profiling notes
- Nsight Systems (timeline): nsight-sys --trace=cuda,nvtx --output=trace.qdrep --processes all --duration=60 -- target-runner
- Nsight Compute (kernel metrics): ncu --set full --target-processes all --export csv kernel_metrics.csv target-runner
- Quick microbenchmark script used: tools/bench/attention_microbench.py --model llama-13b --kernel flashattention|baseline|paged|fused --batch 4 --seq 1024 --device 0
- Key perf counters to watch: achieved sm_efficiency, l2_throughput, dram_utilization, ipc, warp_efficiency
- Repro tips: pin CPU affinity for benchmark runner to avoid scheduler noise; run 5 warmup iterations before measuring; disable power-saver governor.

Notes to reviewers:
- Logs and raw Nsight outputs are stored in s3://redwood-profiling/attention/2026-03/flash-paged-fused/ (link in Confluence).
- The paged-attention code is behind feature-flag in branch attention-profiling-2026-03; be careful merging without retaining flags.
- I intentionally left micro-ops timing tables out of this doc to keep it readable; see kernel_metrics.csv in linked artifacts for per-kernel breakdowns.

If you want, I can extract a short executive bullet summary for PMs and a separate playbook for SREs with rollout checklists.

-- Daniel
